title: OBR: Britain faces 'painful' job losses from AI
content:
British workers face “very, very painful” job losses as AI sweeps through the economy, the chairman of the Office for Budget Responsibility has warned.
Jonathan Haskel said workers should brace for “bad things” as the emerging technology automates more roles.
Mr Haskel said: “AI will displace some people’s jobs, let’s make no bones about that. It’ll be incredibly helpful to other people, on the other hand, and it’s also the case that in all the industrial revolutions we’ve seen thus far, new jobs have been invented and new tasks have come along.
“That can be a very, very painful process, and the idea that it can happen without bad things happening is obviously completely wrong, and we would want people to be helped during that very painful process.”
The comments, made on an Institute for Fiscal Studies podcast, are the starkest warning yet from Britain’s spending watchdog about the negative effects of AI.
Mr Haskel, who previously served on the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee, described himself as a “techno-optimist” and said AI should boost productivity in the economy.
He added: “The first thing is it’s going to improve the productivity of the very innovation process itself. We’re going to invent better medicines and better ways of doing things.
“And the second thing is those improvements are then going to spread out in the economy.”
But those who lose out from the process will need help getting into new jobs, he said, to “make a good transition” to the world of AI.
His comments came after investment in AI was shown to have boosted economic growth, helping GDP expand by 0.7pc in the third quarter of the year.
The Bank of England estimates that around one-fifth of this year’s growth has come from AI spending.
However, the effect on workers’ output has been more limited, and it is expected to take time before businesses and their staff find ways to put the new technology to effective use to improve productivity and living standards.
The rise of the technology has also been blamed for reducing hiring in the economy, as businesses spend money on AI and wait to see which staff they may need in future.
Vacancies at lowest level since Covid
Fewer than 700,000 job vacancies are currently available, according to the Office for National Statistics.
That is the lowest number since the depths of the Covid lockdowns and a figure not seen outside the pandemic since 2014, when the jobs market was still recovering from the financial crisis.
The number of people moving from one job to another has also slumped back to below pre-Covid levels in the past two years, while the situation among young people is at crisis point.
Almost a million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in employment, education or training.
Alan Milburn is set to publish his review of young people and work next week, with recommendations expected to include a reduction in certain benefit payments and an increase in spending on employment support.

report.summary: The OBR chairman warns AI will cause "very, very painful" job losses in Britain, even as AI spending drives a growing share of economic growth.
report.background: AI has become a genuine macroeconomic force in Britain: the Bank of England estimates roughly a fifth of this year's growth came from AI-related spending, helping GDP expand 0.7pc in the third quarter. Yet that boom has not yet translated into worker productivity, which economists say typically lags adoption by years as firms redesign processes and roles. Meanwhile the labour market is softening — vacancies have fallen below 700,000, the lowest since pandemic lockdowns and the weakest non-Covid reading since 2014, and job-to-job moves have dropped below pre-Covid levels. Employers appear to be holding back hiring while they invest in AI and wait to see which roles they still need. Youth unemployment is the sharpest edge of the problem, with almost a million 16- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training — a crisis Alan Milburn's upcoming review is expected to address.
key_points: Jonathan Haskel, chairman of the fiscal watchdog the Office for Budget Responsibility, said AI "will displace some people's jobs, let's make no bones about that", and that the transition will be "very, very painful" for those affected without support.

Haskel, a former Bank of England rate-setter, still calls himself a "techno-optimist": he expects AI to speed up innovation itself — better medicines, better methods — and for those gains to spread across the economy.

The warning lands as the UK budget watchdog's own growth figures show AI spending lifting GDP, but with little measurable effect yet on output per worker, meaning the productivity payoff is lagging the investment boom.
The jobs market is already tightening: vacancies are under 700,000, the lowest since Covid lockdowns, and the number of people switching jobs has fallen back below pre-Covid levels.

Young people are hit hardest, with nearly a million 16- to 24-year-olds not in work, education or training — the focus of Alan Milburn's employment review due next week, expected to pair benefit reform with more spending on employment support.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Haskel's intervention reframes the debate from capability to distribution: expect more political pressure over how AI gains are shared, and possibly incentives or obligations around retraining and workforce transition. For developers and employers, the practical message is that the returns are real but delayed — value will come from redesigning workflows rather than simply substituting tools for headcount, and firms that pause hiring indefinitely may find themselves with skills gaps rather than savings. For regular users and workers, the near-term risk is concentrated in entry-level and routine cognitive roles, exactly where young job-seekers start. The likely policy response looks less like stopping AI and more like active labour-market support, retraining money and tougher conversations about welfare and youth employment.
report.tools: To follow the debate, track OBR publications and its productivity research, Bank of England Monetary Policy Committee minutes and agents' reports on AI adoption, ONS vacancy and NEET datasets, and the IFS podcast where Haskel spoke. The Milburn review, due next week, is the key document on youth employment policy. For hands-on understanding, experiment with open models and agent frameworks (e.g. Hugging Face, LangChain) to see which tasks are genuinely automatable.
